title: SPI-Math Misconception
description: A named, structured student misconception. Misconceptions are the source of truth for multiple-choice distractors and diagnostic feedback. Every distractor on a generated item should reference a misconception by id whenever possible, so that wrong answers are mathematically meaningful rather than arbitrary.

misconceptionId.description: Stable dotted identifier. Convention: MISC.<DOMAIN>.<SHORT_NAME> in upper snake/dotted case.

domain.description: Mathematical domain the misconception belongs to (e.g. 'sequences-and-series', 'fractions').

objectiveRelationships.description: Curriculum objective IDs where this misconception commonly appears.

title.description: Short human-readable title (e.g. 'Off-by-one in term index').

description.description: Plain-English description of the misconception and why students hold it.

observableError.description: What the error looks like in student work or in a final answer.

typicalIncorrectMethod.description: The faulty procedure a student applies, described precisely enough that a distractor rule can implement it.

distractorRule.description: Machine-usable rule for deriving a distractor value from the correct parameters. The actual computation lives in the generator; this documents the intended transformation.

summary.description: e.g. 'Use a1 + n*d instead of a1 + (n-1)*d'.

expression.description: Optional symbolic form of the wrong computation.

validRange.description: Where this misconception is age/course appropriate, so feedback is not shown out of context.

feedback.description: Suitable student-facing feedback when this misconception is detected, phrased constructively.

remediationHint.description: Optional pointer to the correct method or prerequisite skill.

relatedMisconceptions.description: Other misconception IDs that co-occur or are confused with this one.

sourceReferences.description: Source evidence (sourceId + locator) where this misconception was observed or documented.

version.description: Semantic version of this misconception entry.

examples.title: Off-by-one in term index
examples.description: Student treats the first term as term 0, or forgets that the nth term uses (n-1) steps of the common difference.
examples.observableError: Answer is exactly one common difference too large (or small).
examples.typicalIncorrectMethod: Computes a1 + n*d instead of a1 + (n-1)*d.

distractorRule.summary: Use a1 + n*d instead of a1 + (n-1)*d

examples.feedback: Check how many steps of the common difference you take to reach the nth term: it is (n - 1), not n.
examples.remediationHint: List the first few terms and count the jumps from term 1 to term n.
